topic: Feature Skew Silently Breaks Real-Time ML Inference
postText:
Offline training reached 98% precision. On paper, our patient risk prioritization model was ready for deployment.

Then real-time traffic hit the hospital intake, and clinical predictions drifted wildly.

Root cause: Training-serving feature skew.

In the offline environment, data scientists computed 30-day vitals aggregations via batch SQL queries over historical database tables. In production, our low-latency inference service pulled recent vitals from a Redis cache and streaming stream processors in real-time.

A slight mismatch in sliding window edge calculations created completely divergent input vectors for the exact same clinical state. The model did not throw exceptions; it silently produced low-confidence or incorrect inferences on valid data.

To eradicate feature skew in mission-critical ML systems, three architectural rules are essential:

1. Unified Feature Pipeline: Train and serve features must share the exact same transformation code, eliminating discrepancies between batch and streaming runtimes.
2. Point-In-Time Correctness: Implement strict temporal joins during training dataset construction to prevent future leakage.
3. Continuous Drift Detection: Log real-time feature inputs alongside model inference results and monitor against offline baseline distributions via telemetry.

Production ML fails silently on skewed feature contracts, not code crashes.

How do you guarantee feature consistency between offline training datasets and low-latency inference services in your architecture?
